rv.q: A significantly more confident and sexier iteration of Josie Rourke's production.

"The formidable McTeer has made the leap and so has the taut direction by the Donmar’s Artistic Director Josie Rourke. Liev Schreiber makes a welcome, languid return to Broadway with more than enough chemistry with his co-star...
Schreiber may never seem inevitably to the manor born.
No mere scheming temptress, this Merteuil is driven by a ferocious desire for independence and contempt for sexual hypocrisy that remain bracingly current.
This revival simply crackles as a witty comedy descends into horrific satire.
Josie Rourke’s evocative staging provides a compelling portrait of a dissolute aristocracy on the brink of devouring itself.
Schreiber's impassive libertine pairs nicely with McTeer's vengeful, wicked widow.
In the same parts, Ms. McTeer and Mr. Schreiber come across as magnificent bulls who have strayed into a Limoges china shop.
In this version, which originated at London’s Donmar Warehouse under the direction of its artistic director, Josie Rourke, wit and style count more than passion.
In all, it’s an oddly off-putting mix of period melodrama and contemporary finger-wagging that left me unmoved and deflated for all the wrong reasons.
This plodding, dull production does not seem to understand the pitfalls of that particular scene, and thus does not do enough to remediate those concerns.
The acting is consistently unsubtle and unfunny
The director extracts witty, erotically charged and deeply moving performances, and not just from the two leads.

What initially seemed to me to be a less-than-necessary revival – this is the show’s third Broadway outing, plus there are two major film versions -- turns out to be required viewing for serious theatergoers.
For the bulk of this nearly three hour drama, it’s great entertainment watching these unparalleled actors hiss and feed on each other like a pair of insatiable snakes.
The show runs only through January, a “strictly limited engagement” – which is a fairly accurate summary of my reaction to it.
Soporific turns aside, this revival production makes an airtight case that Les Liaisons Dangereuses is a play for our depraved age.
In modern times, you might hover over its image for a few fleeting seconds, but eventually swipe left, looking for the next potential lover to strike your fancy.
As presented here, the Hampton play turns into another of those British middle-brow dramas masquerading as high art.
Tepid because most of these performances are without luster.
Director Josie Rourke has managed to take the fun and suspense out of this well-made drama through bad casting and design choices, leaving a disjointed, dull and dragging production.
What a delight, then, that the Donmar Warehouse has imported a production worthy of Christopher Hampton’s text.
McTeer, a true master of the stage, gives us a woman in full control of each and every devious turn.
That difference diminishes the impact of the events in the second act, leaving the play’s cleverness intact but its passions practically nonexistent.
Which doesn‘t mean it‘s not entertaining, just not high drama.
And so, too, is the rest of the play distant: Stagey and self-consciously acted, never rich and emotionally resonant.
For three hours Josie Rourke fails to bring the play to life.

cn.t: Critics are sharply divided on this revival: McTeer earns widespread praise for her blazing performance, but many fault Schreiber's miscast Valmont and question the production's necessity, finding it stylish yet lacking the danger and moral complexity the material demands.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
